mountains-moving.title: Mountains That Pass Like Clouds
mountains-moving.hook: “You see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds”: mountains really are moving.
mountains-moving.science.0: Mountains feel like the most fixed things there are, yet the ground is carried by the Earth's spin at up to 1,670 km/h at the equator without our feeling it. In 1851 Léon Foucault's pendulum made that turning visible.
mountains-moving.science.1: The mountains also travel on drifting plates. India is moving north into Asia at about 4–5 cm a year, pushing the Himalaya up by about half a centimetre a year. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, and the 1960s brought the theory of plate tectonics; GPS stations now measure the motion directly.
mountains-moving.stats.0.label: Speed of the ground at the equator from the Earth's spin
mountains-moving.stats.1.label: Speed of India moving into Asia
mountains-moving.stats.2.label: Foucault's pendulum shows the Earth turning
mountains-moving.proof.0.title: Foucault's pendulum
mountains-moving.proof.0.text: Léon Foucault hangs a long pendulum in the Panthéon in Paris. Its plane of swing slowly rotates: the Earth is turning beneath it.
mountains-moving.proof.0.cap: A Foucault pendulum, which shows the Earth turning.
mountains-moving.proof.1.title: Wegener: continents drift
mountains-moving.proof.1.text: Alfred Wegener proposes that the continents were once joined and have drifted apart. Most geologists reject the idea for decades.
mountains-moving.proof.2.title: Plate tectonics
mountains-moving.proof.2.text: Mapping of the sea floor, bands of magnetism in the rocks on either side of ocean ridges and patterns of earthquakes show that the Earth's surface is made of moving plates.
mountains-moving.proof.3.title: GPS on the mountains
mountains-moving.proof.3.text: GPS stations across the Himalaya and Tibet measure India moving north into Asia at about 4–5 cm a year.
mountains-moving.fit.0: Mountains that look solid are carried along by the Earth's spin and by drifting plates, and “passing like clouds” fits a smooth motion we cannot feel.
mountains-moving.gap.0: Most commentators read the verse as describing the Day of Judgment, when the mountains pass away.
mountains-moving.gap.1: “Like clouds” suggests swift, effortless motion; plate motion is centimetres a year.
mountains-moving.gap.2: That the Earth turns had been argued by earlier astronomers; the verse is not a statement of plate tectonics.
mountains-moving.media.0.cap: A Foucault pendulum, which shows the Earth turning.
sky-returns.title: The Sky That Returns
sky-returns.hook: “By the sky that returns”: the sky sends back rain, and even radio waves.
sky-returns.science.0: The sky returns things to the Earth. Water evaporates, rises and comes back as rain, year after year. About 30% of the sunlight that reaches the Earth is sent straight back to space by clouds, air and surface.
sky-returns.science.1: High in the atmosphere, a layer of charged gas, the ionosphere, bounces radio waves back down. In 1901 Guglielmo Marconi sent a radio signal across the Atlantic, over the curve of the Earth. In 1902 Oliver Heaviside and Arthur Kennelly proposed that a reflecting layer must exist, and Edward Appleton and Miles Barnett proved it in 1924 (Nobel Prize 1947).
sky-returns.stats.0.label: Sunlight the Earth sends straight back to space
sky-returns.stats.1.label: First radio signal across the Atlantic
sky-returns.stats.2.label: Ionosphere proved by Appleton and Barnett
sky-returns.proof.0.title: Marconi: across the Atlantic
sky-returns.proof.0.text: Guglielmo Marconi sends a radio signal from Cornwall to Newfoundland, over the curve of the Earth, when many physicists thought radio waves must travel in straight lines.
sky-returns.proof.1.title: Heaviside and Kennelly: a reflecting layer
sky-returns.proof.1.text: Oliver Heaviside and Arthur Kennelly independently propose that a layer of electrically charged gas high in the atmosphere reflects radio waves back to the ground.
sky-returns.proof.2.title: Appleton and Barnett: proved
sky-returns.proof.2.text: Edward Appleton and Miles Barnett show by experiment that radio waves are reflected from the upper atmosphere: the ionosphere exists. Appleton wins the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physics.
sky-returns.proof.3.title: Earth's return of sunlight
sky-returns.proof.3.text: NASA's Earth Radiation Budget Experiment measures how much sunlight the Earth reflects back to space: about 30%.
sky-returns.fit.0: Classical commentators, such as Ibn ʿAbbās, read rajʿ as rain that returns time after time: the water cycle.
sky-returns.fit.1: “The returning” also fits a sky that sends back radio waves and sunlight.
sky-returns.gap.0: The radio reading is modern; the classical reading is rain.
sky-returns.gap.1: Rajʿ says only “return” and does not say what returns.
sky-returns.gap.2: Some early commentators read it as the cycle of the Sun and Moon.
sky-returns.media.1.cap: The ionosphere and thermosphere high above the Earth (NASA).
oldest-manuscripts.title: Written Down 1,400 Years Ago
oldest-manuscripts.hook: “We will be its guardian.” Pages carbon-dated to 568–645 CE carry the same verses, in the same order, that are recited today.
oldest-manuscripts.science.0: In 2015 the University of Birmingham had two parchment leaves from its Mingana Collection radiocarbon-dated at the University of Oxford. The result was 568–645 CE with 95.4% probability: the animal whose skin became the page lived in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ (c. 570–632) or within a few years of it.
oldest-manuscripts.science.1: The leaves hold parts of Surahs 18, 19 and 20 in the early Hijazi script. Their verses are in the order recited today and conform to the standard text. They come from the same manuscript as 16 leaves kept in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris.
oldest-manuscripts.science.2: They are not alone. A fragment at the University of Tübingen (Ma VI 165) was dated to 649–675 CE in 2014. The Sanaa palimpsest, part of a cache found in 1972 in the Great Mosque of Sanaa, Yemen, was dated to 578–669 CE.
oldest-manuscripts.stats.0.label: Birmingham leaves, radiocarbon date (95.4%)
oldest-manuscripts.stats.1.label: Tübingen fragment, radiocarbon date
oldest-manuscripts.stats.2.label: Sanaa manuscripts found in a mosque attic
oldest-manuscripts.proof.0.title: A hidden cache in Sanaa
oldest-manuscripts.proof.0.text: Workers repairing the attic of the Great Mosque of Sanaa, Yemen, find large quantities of old parchment. By 1997 the fragments had been sorted into 926 separate Quran manuscripts.
oldest-manuscripts.proof.1.title: The Sanaa palimpsest is dated
oldest-manuscripts.proof.1.text: Behnam Sadeghi and Uwe Bergmann publish a radiocarbon date for one of its leaves: 578–669 CE with 95% probability. Its visible upper text is the standard text; an older, erased lower text differs from it in places.
oldest-manuscripts.proof.1.cap: A leaf of the Sanaa palimpsest.
oldest-manuscripts.proof.2.title: Tübingen
oldest-manuscripts.proof.2.text: The University of Tübingen announces that its Quran fragment Ma VI 165 dates to 649–675 CE (95.4%).
oldest-manuscripts.proof.3.title: Birmingham
oldest-manuscripts.proof.3.text: While studying the Mingana Collection for her PhD, Alba Fedeli notices two leaves in an early script. Oxford's Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit measures 1465 ± 21 radiocarbon years: 568–645 CE with 95.4% probability.
oldest-manuscripts.proof.4.title: Part of a Paris codex
oldest-manuscripts.proof.4.text: François Déroche confirms that the Birmingham leaves belong with 16 leaves in Paris, now bound with the Codex Parisino-petropolitanus.
oldest-manuscripts.fit.0: Several manuscripts from the first Islamic century survive, and their text is recognisably the Quran recited today.
oldest-manuscripts.fit.1: The Birmingham leaves have their verses in today's order, and Marijn van Putten has shown they share the spelling quirks of the ʿUthmānic text.
oldest-manuscripts.fit.2: The verse promises the Reminder will be guarded, and copies from its first decades support the tradition that the text was fixed early.
oldest-manuscripts.gap.0: Radiocarbon dates the death of the animal, not the day of writing. Parchment could be stored first, so the Birmingham text may have been written as late as the 650s.
oldest-manuscripts.gap.1: Some specialists, including François Déroche, doubt how precise radiocarbon dates of Qurans are.
oldest-manuscripts.gap.2: The erased lower text of the Sanaa palimpsest has real differences from the standard text, including extra words and a different order of surahs.
oldest-manuscripts.gap.3: The earliest copies have no vowel marks and few dots. They preserve the consonant outline; the exact recitation was passed on orally.
oldest-manuscripts.media.0.cap: The Birmingham leaves: the end of Surah 19 and the start of Surah 20 (left), and Surah 18 (right).
oldest-manuscripts.media.1.cap: A leaf of the Sanaa palimpsest. An older, erased text lies beneath the visible one.
oldest-manuscripts.media.2.cap: The first page of the Codex Parisino-petropolitanus in Paris, which the Birmingham leaves belong with.
saba-dam.title: The Flood of the Dam
saba-dam.hook: Saba' had “two gardens, on the right and on the left”, until “the flood of the dam”. The dam, and the two oases on either side of it, were real.
saba-dam.proofH: What the inscriptions and ruins record
saba-dam.science.0: The Sabaeans of Yemen built a great earth dam upstream of their capital, Maʾrib, to catch the monsoon floods. Its earliest inscription names the ruler Yathaʿ ʾAmar Watar I, who reigned about 760–740 BCE. Around 500 BCE the dam was raised and irrigation was extended from the northern side of the valley to the southern side as well: two oases, one on each side.
saba-dam.science.1: At its height the dam stood 14 metres high, with sluices at both ends, and watered about 100 km² of fields. Inscriptions record breaches in 449, 450, 542 and 548 CE and costly repairs, the last in 557. In 570 or 575 the water overtopped it again, and this time it was never repaired. The fields died and many people left Yemen.
saba-dam.stats.0.label: Reign named in the earliest dam inscription
saba-dam.stats.1.label: Fields the dam watered
saba-dam.stats.2.label: Final breach, never repaired
saba-dam.proof.0.title: The first inscription
saba-dam.proof.0.text: An inscription placed on the dam during building or repair names the Sabaean ruler Yathaʿ ʾAmar Watar I.
saba-dam.proof.0.cap: Remains of the ancient dam of Maʾrib.
saba-dam.proof.1.title: Two gardens
saba-dam.proof.1.text: The dam is raised to 7 metres and faced with stone, and irrigation is extended to the southern side of the valley as well as the northern: two oases, one on each side.
saba-dam.proof.2.title: Breaches and repairs
saba-dam.proof.2.text: Inscriptions record major breaches in 449, 450, 542 and 548, the workers and the costs of repair, and a last repair in 557. The ruler Abraha repairs much of Maʾrib's works around 548.
saba-dam.proof.3.title: The last flood
saba-dam.proof.3.text: The water overtops the dam again, and it is left unrepaired. The irrigation system fails and many people migrate across Arabia.
saba-dam.proof.4.title: World Heritage
saba-dam.proof.4.text: UNESCO lists the landmarks of the ancient Kingdom of Saba, Maʾrib, as World Heritage, and at once as in danger because of the war in Yemen.
saba-dam.fit.0: Saba' was a real kingdom centred on Maʾrib, and its dam was one of the engineering wonders of the ancient world.
saba-dam.fit.1: The watered land lay in two oases on either side of the valley: “two gardens, on the right and on the left”.
saba-dam.fit.2: The dam did fail and was abandoned, and its gardens went back to desert scrub.
saba-dam.gap.0: Which breach the verse means is debated: a major breach in about 145 BCE, or the final one in 570 or 575.
saba-dam.gap.1: The fall of Saba' was well known to Arabs in the Prophet's ﷺ time. This is history that checks out, not hidden knowledge.
saba-dam.gap.2: The verses give a moral reason (they turned away). Archaeology can confirm the flood, not the reason.
saba-dam.media.0.cap: Remains of the ancient dam of Maʾrib, Yemen.
saba-dam.media.1.cap: Ruins of ancient Maʾrib, the capital of Saba'.
thamud.title: Thamud, Named in Stone
thamud.hook: The Quran speaks of Thamud, a people of north-west Arabia who carved homes from rock. Assyrian, Greek and Roman-era records name them too.
thamud.proofH: Where Thamud appear in the records
thamud.science.0: The annals of the Assyrian king Sargon II (reigned 722–705 BCE), inscribed at his palace at Dur-Sharrukin, list Thamud among the Arabian tribes he says he defeated. Greek and Roman writers knew them too: Diodorus in the 1st century BCE, Pliny in the 1st century CE and Ptolemy in the 2nd.
thamud.science.1: At Ruwāfa in north-west Arabia, about 200 km north-west of Hegra, a temple carries inscriptions in Greek and Nabataean from 165–169 CE. They say “the Thamud” built it, in honour of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Thamud troops still served Rome in the 5th century.
thamud.science.2: Islamic tradition identifies the “companions of al-Ḥijr” (15:80) with Thamud and places them at Hegra, also called Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ. More than 110 tombs are cut into its sandstone cliffs; they were carved by the Nabataeans about 2,000 years ago.
thamud.stats.0.label: Reign of Sargon II, whose annals name Thamud
thamud.stats.1.label: Ruwāfa temple built by the Thamud
thamud.stats.2.label: Rock-cut tombs at Hegra (Nabataean)
thamud.proof.0.title: Sargon II's annals
thamud.proof.0.text: The Assyrian king's annals, inscribed at Dur-Sharrukin, list Thamud among Arab tribes he says he defeated and moved to Samaria. The historian Israel Ephʿal doubts the campaign happened as told, but the name is there.
thamud.proof.1.title: Greek and Roman writers
thamud.proof.1.text: Diodorus places the Thamudeni on the Red Sea coast of Arabia; Pliny and Ptolemy mention them too.
thamud.proof.2.title: The Ruwāfa temple
thamud.proof.2.text: Alois Musil finds a temple in the Hisma desert with inscriptions in Greek and Nabataean. Dated to 165–169 CE, they say the Thamud built it under Roman rule.
thamud.proof.3.title: Hegra, World Heritage
thamud.proof.3.text: UNESCO makes Hegra (al-Ḥijr, Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ) Saudi Arabia's first World Heritage Site. Its rock-cut tombs are Nabataean.
thamud.fit.0: Thamud were a real people of north-west Arabia, named in records from the 8th century BCE to the 5th century CE.
thamud.fit.1: Their region, around al-Ḥijr, is full of rooms and tombs cut into rock: the kind of place the verses describe.
thamud.gap.0: The famous tombs at Hegra were carved by the Nabataeans, not by the older Thamud. Archaeologists have not identified Thamud's own rock houses.
thamud.gap.1: Sargon II's account may be exaggerated, and the destruction of Thamud is told only in scripture.
thamud.gap.2: Arabs in the Prophet's ﷺ time passed Hegra on the caravan road, so Thamud's name was known. This is history that checks out, not hidden knowledge.
thamud.media.0.cap: A tomb cut into the rock at Hegra (al-Ḥijr), carved by the Nabataeans.
thamud.media.1.cap: Sargon II of Assyria, whose annals name Thamud (relief from Dur-Sharrukin, c. 716–713 BCE).
appointed-term.title: The Sun Has an Appointed Term
appointed-term.hook: The Sun and the Moon each run “for an appointed term”. Physics found that the Sun's fuel is limited, and measured how long it will last.
appointed-term.science.0: Why does the Sun shine, and for how long? Around 1920 Arthur Eddington was the first to suggest, correctly, that stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium. In 1939 Hans Bethe worked out the nuclear reactions that do it, and won the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physics.
appointed-term.science.1: Fusion uses up the Sun's hydrogen. The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago; the oldest material in the Solar System is 4.567 billion years old. In about 5 billion years, helium building up in its core will end its steady life. It will swell into a red giant, shed its outer layers and end as a white dwarf that no longer produces energy by fusion.
appointed-term.science.2: The Moon's course is changing too. Lasers bounced off mirrors left on the Moon show it spiralling away from the Earth by 3.8 cm a year.
appointed-term.stats.0.label: The Sun's age so far
appointed-term.stats.1.label: Until it leaves its steady phase
appointed-term.stats.2.label: The Moon's drift away from Earth
appointed-term.proof.0.title: Eddington: hydrogen into helium
appointed-term.proof.0.text: In “The Internal Constitution of the Stars”, Arthur Eddington suggests the Sun shines by fusing hydrogen into helium. At the time the source of starlight was a complete mystery.
appointed-term.proof.1.title: Bethe: the reactions
appointed-term.proof.1.text: Hans Bethe works out the nuclear reactions that power the Sun and other stars (Physical Review 55, 434). He wins the 1967 Nobel Prize.
appointed-term.proof.2.title: Measuring the Moon
appointed-term.proof.2.text: Lasers fired at reflectors left on the Moon, starting with Apollo 11, time the round trip of light and show the Moon spiralling away by 3.8 cm a year.
appointed-term.proof.3.title: The age of the Solar System
appointed-term.proof.3.text: Lead isotopes in the oldest grains of meteorites give an age of 4.567 billion years (Connelly et al., Science 338).
appointed-term.fit.0: “Each runs for an appointed term”: the Sun has a limited supply of fuel and a lifetime that can be calculated.
appointed-term.fit.1: 81:1 speaks of the Sun being “wrapped up”, and physics expects the Sun's light as we know it to end.
appointed-term.gap.0: Classical commentators read the “term” as the Day of Judgement, or as the Sun's daily and yearly course.
appointed-term.gap.1: 81:1 describes the Last Day, not a red giant billions of years from now. Nothing in the verses gives a timescale.
appointed-term.gap.2: That the Sun and Moon will not last forever is a belief of many religions and philosophies, not only a result of physics.
appointed-term.media.0.cap: The Sun in ultraviolet light (NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory).
appointed-term.media.1.cap: The Sun today, compared with the red giant it will become.
cosmic-web.title: A Sky Woven With Paths
cosmic-web.hook: “By the sky full of pathways (ḥubuk).” Maps of the galaxies show them strung along a vast web of filaments.
cosmic-web.science.0: In 1986 Valérie de Lapparent, Margaret Geller and John Huchra mapped the galaxies in a thin slice of sky. Instead of a random scatter, the galaxies lay on the walls of huge bubbles around empty voids. In 1989 Geller and Huchra found the “Great Wall”, a sheet of galaxies stretching across their map.
cosmic-web.science.1: Bigger surveys and computer simulations, such as the Millennium Simulation of 2005, showed the whole universe is built this way: a “cosmic web” of filaments of galaxies and gas crossing between clusters, with voids in between. Gravity alone pulls matter into this pattern.
cosmic-web.science.2: The filaments are mostly invisible gas and dark matter. In 2019 a team led by Hideki Umehata captured the faint glow of cosmic-web gas directly, in a young cluster of galaxies whose light set out more than 11 billion years ago.
cosmic-web.stats.0.label: First “slice of the universe” map
cosmic-web.stats.1.label: The Great Wall of galaxies
cosmic-web.stats.2.label: Web gas seen directly
cosmic-web.disc.who: de Lapparent, Geller & Huchra · Springel et al. · Umehata et al.
cosmic-web.proof.0.title: A slice of the universe
cosmic-web.proof.0.text: de Lapparent, Geller and Huchra map the galaxies in a thin wedge of sky. They sit on the walls of bubbles around empty voids (Astrophysical Journal 302, L1).
cosmic-web.proof.1.title: The Great Wall
cosmic-web.proof.1.text: Geller and Huchra report a vast wall of galaxies stretching across their map (Science 246, 897).
cosmic-web.proof.2.title: The Millennium Simulation
cosmic-web.proof.2.text: Volker Springel and colleagues follow 10 billion particles of dark matter in a supercomputer. Gravity draws them into a web of filaments (Nature 435, 629).
cosmic-web.proof.2.cap: The cosmic web in the Millennium Simulation (Springel, Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics).
cosmic-web.proof.3.title: The web seen
cosmic-web.proof.3.text: Hideki Umehata and colleagues detect glowing gas in filaments that link galaxies in the young cluster SSA22 (Science 366, 97).
cosmic-web.fit.0: Ḥubuk means paths or tracks, and also a weave or well-knit structure: the galaxies lie along filaments like threads.
cosmic-web.fit.1: The verse swears by the structure of the sky, and the large-scale structure of the universe was unknown until the 1980s.
cosmic-web.gap.0: Classical commentators read ḥubuk as the sky's beauty and fine making, the courses of the stars, or ripples like wind on sand.
cosmic-web.gap.1: The cosmic web can only be seen with telescopes and computers. The verse speaks to people looking up at the night sky.
cosmic-web.gap.2: “Paths” could describe many things in the sky, so the match is suggestive rather than specific.
cosmic-web.media.0.cap: A simulated cosmic web (Illustris): dark matter in blue, gas in orange, gathered along filaments around voids.
cosmic-web.media.1.cap: The 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey: each dot is a galaxy, and they line up in threads and walls.
cosmic-web.media.2.cap: A filament of the cosmic web imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope.
